name: Words trivia (medium)
description: 50 medium questions about word meanings, origins, spelling, idioms, grammar. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: A contronym, a word that is its own opposite, is also called a "Janus word" after a Roman god. What is that god usually shown with?
items.explain: Janus word comes from the Roman god Janus, who is usually depicted with two faces, like a word with two opposite meanings.

source.title: Contronym - Wikipedia

items.question: Which verb can mean both "to officially approve" and "to impose penalties on"?
items.explain: Sanction is a common contronym. A government can sanction a country by punishing it, or sanction a policy by approving it.

source.title: Contronym - Definition, Meaning & Synonyms - Vocabulary.com

items.question: Which everyday verb can mean either to cover something with fine particles or to remove fine particles from it?
items.explain: Dust is a contronym. You can dust a rolling pin with flour, or dust a bookshelf to remove dust.

source.title: Contronym - Definition, Meaning & Synonyms - Vocabulary.com

items.question: Why does the verb "cleave" mean both "to split apart" and "to stick closely"?
answers: It merged two separate Old English words
It was once spelled backwards in Latin
It came from a medieval legal term
It was altered by Shakespeare's plays
items.correct: It merged two separate Old English words
items.explain: Cleave comes from two different Old English words, clēofan and cleofian. They ended up with one modern spelling and opposite meanings.

source.title: Contronyms You've Been Using Without Realizing It - Thesaurus.com

items.question: Who coined the term "portmanteau word" for a blend of two words, in Through the Looking-Glass (1871)?
items.explain: Lewis Carroll first applied the luggage term "portmanteau" to combined words in Through the Looking-Glass.

source.title: Portmanteau - Wikipedia

items.question: Lewis Carroll coined "chortle" in "Jabberwocky". Which two words is it likely a blend of?
items.explain: Chortle is likely a portmanteau of "chuckle" and "snort".

source.title: 'Slithy,' 'chortle,' and other portmanteau words - CSMonitor.com

items.question: In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty explains that "slithy" means "lithe and" which other adjective?
items.explain: Humpty Dumpty says "slithy" means "lithe and slimy", which he compares to a portmanteau with two meanings packed into one word.

source.title: The Frabjous Words Invented By Lewis Carroll - Dictionary.com

items.question: Before Lewis Carroll applied it to words, what did "portmanteau" literally refer to?
answers: A cloak with a built-in hood
A suitcase hinged in two halves
items.correct: A suitcase hinged in two halves
items.explain: A portmanteau was an old-style suitcase made of two halves hinged together. Carroll used it as an image for two meanings packed into one word.

source.title: Portmanteau words - Macquarie Dictionary

items.question: The word "podcast" is a portmanteau of "broadcast" and the name of which product?
items.explain: Podcast blends the brand name iPod with broadcast.

source.title: What is a Portmanteau Word? - Interesting Literature

items.question: The English word "salary" comes from Latin "salarium", a derivative of the Latin word for which substance?
items.explain: Salarium derives from sal, "salt". The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt goes back to Pliny, but modern scholars doubt it.

source.title: SALARY Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

items.question: The term "malapropism" comes from a character in which 1775 play by Richard Brinsley Sheridan?
items.explain: Mrs Malaprop, who misuses words, is a character in Sheridan's 1775 play The Rivals.

source.title: Malapropism - Wikipedia

items.question: Sheridan took the name "Malaprop" from a French term. What does that term, "mal à propos", mean?
items.explain: Sheridan took the name from the French mal à propos, meaning "inappropriate".

source.title: MALAPROPISM Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

items.question: Mrs Malaprop praises a young man as "the very pineapple of politeness". Which word did she mean to say?
items.explain: Mrs Malaprop's "pineapple" is a mistake for "pinnacle". It is the classic example of a malapropism.

source.title: Malapropism - Encyclopedia.com

items.question: Spoonerisms, which swap the opening sounds of words, are named after which Oxford clergyman and academic?
items.explain: The Reverend William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930) was an Oxford don who was reputed to make such slips.

source.title: Spoonerism - Wikipedia

items.question: Which phrase is a classic spoonerism of "our dear old Queen"?
items.explain: Swapping the opening sounds of "dear" and "Queen" gives "queer old dean", the example attributed to Spooner.

source.title: What is a Spoonerism — Definition & Examples Explained - StudioBinder

items.question: William Spooner, the man behind "spoonerism", was Warden of which Oxford college?
items.explain: Spooner was Warden of New College, Oxford.

source.title: Spoonerism - Definition and Examples - Poem Analysis

items.question: Which wordplay form, in which the writer avoids one or more letters, is described as the opposite of a pangram?
items.explain: A pangram uses every letter of the alphabet, while a lipogram deliberately omits one or more letters.

source.title: PANGRAM - Cambridge Dictionary

items.question: Which lipogrammatic novel by Mark Dunn is built around the "quick brown fox" pangram?
items.explain: Mark Dunn's Ella Minnow Pea is built around the "quick brown fox" pangram and its inventor.

source.title: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog - Wikipedia

items.question: Which author's 1891 novel The Light That Failed contains the first known figurative use of "bite the bullet"?
items.explain: The first known written use of "bite the bullet" as an idiom is in Rudyard Kipling's 1891 book The Light That Failed.

source.title: Bite the Bullet – Meaning, Origin & Usage

items.question: The Library of Congress lists several theories for "raining cats and dogs". Which one does it label a false theory?
answers: A Greek phrase for "contrary to belief"
Pets washed out of thatched roofs
items.correct: Pets washed out of thatched roofs
items.explain: The Library of Congress calls the idea that cats and dogs cuddled in thatch and were washed out a false theory. The other explanations it lists are suggestions from etymologists.

source.title: What is the origin of the phrase "it's raining cats and dogs?" - Library of Congress

items.question: The idiom "spill the beans" is said to come from an ancient practice of doing what with beans?
answers: Voting by placing them in jars
items.correct: Voting by placing them in jars
items.explain: The phrase is said to originate from an ancient voting method in which beans were deposited in jars. A spilled jar would reveal the result early.

source.title: Idiom - Wikipedia

items.question: The cardigan is named after the 7th Earl of Cardigan, who wore a buttoned wool garment while leading what in 1854?
answers: The Charge of the Light Brigade
items.correct: The Charge of the Light Brigade
items.explain: James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan, led the famous Charge of the Light Brigade in the Crimean War, and the sweater took his title.

source.title: Are 'sandwich' and 'cardigan' named after real people? - CSMonitor.com

items.question: The word "boycott" comes from a land agent who was ostracized by tenants in which country?
items.explain: Captain Charles C. Boycott was a land agent who was ostracized by the Irish for his poor treatment of them.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning and Popular Examples - YourDictionary

items.question: Which women's rights activist gave her name to a type of garment?
items.explain: Bloomers take their name from women's rights activist Amelia Bloomer.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning and Popular Examples - YourDictionary

items.question: "Sideburns" are named after a general famous for his facial hair. Who was he?
items.explain: Sideburns are an eponym from General Ambrose Burnside, who had impressive facial hair.

source.title: English eponyms revealed: Words named after people

items.question: The Caesar salad is named after which person?
items.explain: The salad is named for the chef and restaurateur Caesar Cardini, not the Roman ruler.

source.title: English eponyms revealed: Words named after people

items.question: "Nicotine" is named after which man, who introduced tobacco to France?
items.explain: Nicotine takes its name from Jean Nicot, who introduced tobacco to France.

source.title: 50 Words Named After People: The Fascinating World of Eponyms

items.question: The word "mausoleum" comes from the name of which ruler, whose grand tomb became one of the Seven Wonders?
items.explain: Mausoleum comes from Mausolus, a Persian satrap whose grand tomb became one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

source.title: 50 Words Named After People: The Fascinating World of Eponyms

items.question: The word "maverick" comes from the surname of Samuel Maverick. What was he?
items.explain: Maverick is an eponym from the rancher Samuel Maverick.

source.title: 15 Everyday Words That Are Named After Real People

items.question: The word "algorithm" derives from the name of which medieval mathematician?
items.explain: Algorithm is an eponym from the mathematician al-Khwārizmī.

source.title: Eponyms — Words Named After Real People

items.question: The Greek roots of "oxymoron" combine which two meanings?
items.explain: Oxymoron comes from Greek oxys, "sharp, keen", and mōros, "foolish", so it literally means "pointedly foolish".

source.title: OXYMORON Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

items.question: Which everyday word shares its Greek root meaning "foolish" with "oxymoron"?
items.explain: Both oxymoron and moron come from the Greek word mōros, meaning "foolish".

source.title: OXYMORON Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

items.question: Which of these is an accepted plural of "oxymoron"?
items.explain: Merriam-Webster gives the plural as oxymorons or oxymora.

source.title: OXYMORON Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

items.question: The Greek origin of "onomatopoeia" means roughly what?
items.explain: Onomatopoeia comes from Ancient Greek onoma ("name") plus poiéō ("making"), meaning "name-making".

source.title: Onomatopoeia - Wikipedia

items.question: In the list "pancakes, scrambled eggs, and bacon", which comma is the Oxford comma?
answers: There is none in this list
items.explain: The Oxford (serial) comma is the comma placed before the conjunction in a list of three or more items.

source.title: Serial Comma | Rules, Examples & Definition - Scribbr

items.question: Besides "serial comma", what other name is the Oxford comma known by?
items.explain: The serial comma is also called the Oxford comma or the Harvard comma.

source.title: Serial Comma | Rules, Examples & Definition - Scribbr

items.question: Shakespeare is credited with the word "alligator". In which of his plays does it appear?
items.explain: The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust's list of coined words credits "alligator" to Romeo and Juliet.

source.title: Shakespeare's invented words - Shakespeare Birthplace Trust

items.question: Shakespeare is credited with first using "lonely" in which play?
items.explain: Shakespeare was the first to use the word "lonely", in Coriolanus.

source.title: 20 words and phrases you didn't know Shakespeare invented - EF GO Blog

items.question: In Othello, Shakespeare's "addiction" described a state of being what?
items.explain: In Othello, "addiction" meant being dedicated or devoted to a thing. It was not yet tied to bad habits.

source.title: 50 Common Words Invented by Shakespeare We Still Use Today

items.question: Shakespeare's "bandit" comes from an Italian word for people who had been what?
items.explain: "Bandit" comes from the Italian word for people who were "banned", meaning outlaws.

source.title: Shakespeare's invented words - Shakespeare Birthplace Trust

items.question: "Algebra" comes from the Arabic "al-jabr". What did that term refer to?
items.explain: Al-jabr means the restoration of broken parts, an idea of restoring balance from 9th-century Arabic mathematics.

source.title: 10 English Words With Arabic Origins - TheCollector

items.question: The word "zero" traces back to an Arabic word, "sifr". What did it mean?
items.explain: Fibonacci took the Arabic sifr, meaning "empty" or "nothing", and Latinized it, and it became our word zero.

source.title: 15 English words we stole from Arabic - The Week

items.question: Which Italian mathematician introduced zero to Europeans in the early 1200s, having learned it in North Africa?
items.explain: Fibonacci learned the idea of zero from Arabic culture in North Africa and introduced it to Europe in the early 1200s.

source.title: 15 English words we stole from Arabic - The Week

items.question: "Alcohol" comes from the Arabic "al-kuhl". What did that term originally refer to?
items.explain: Al-kuḥl originally referred to a fine cosmetic powder before its meaning evolved over time.

source.title: How Arabic helped shape everyday English - UCLA Newsroom

items.question: In English words borrowed from Arabic, such as "alcove" and "alchemy", what does the prefix "al-" mean?
items.explain: The Arabic prefix al- is the definite article, meaning "the", and many borrowed words kept it.

source.title: 10 English Words With Arabic Origins - TheCollector

items.question: Which of these household words came into English from Arabic?
items.explain: The Week lists mattress, along with sofa, among everyday English words that came from Arabic.

source.title: 15 English words we stole from Arabic - The Week

items.question: According to the Macquarie Dictionary's list, what is a group of leopards called?
items.explain: Macquarie's list of collective nouns for animals gives "leap" for leopards.

source.title: Common Collective Nouns for Animals - Macquarie Dictionary

items.question: What is the collective noun for a group of crocodiles?
items.explain: A group of crocodiles is called a bask.

source.title: Animal Group Names: Collective Nouns for Animals

items.question: Many animal collective nouns trace back to which 1486 English book on hawking, hunting and heraldry?
items.explain: These terms can be traced to the fifteenth century, when they were first published in The Book of St Albans (1486).

source.title: A Murder of Crows, and other collective nouns for animal groups

items.question: One theory says "cats and dogs" in "raining cats and dogs" corrupts the obsolete word "catadupe". What did that word mean?
items.explain: The Library of Congress says "cats and dogs" may be a perversion of the obsolete word catadupe, meaning waterfall.

source.title: What is the origin of the phrase "it's raining cats and dogs?" - Library of Congress
